(CNN)  -- Is the movie cop thriller heading for retirement? Colin Farrell, left, and Edward Norton star in "Pride and Glory" as New York cops. Based on a video game, "Max Payne" takes a rudimentary plot and boils it down still further, to the point where it's worse than predictable. The film's attraction (such as it is) isn't found in story, but in decoration: the blue-filtered chiaroscuro and etch-y comic book compositions, how the snow glints under the streetlights. Watch behind the scenes at "Pride and Glory" » . The time period isn't specified, but it seems to be today, going on 1974. Written by "Tumbleweeds" director Gavin O'Connor and Joe Carnahan ("Narc"), based on a story O'Connor put together with his twin brother Greg and ex-New York cop Robert Hopes, this is one of those movies that wants to emulate the serious side of '70s cinema, to dig into thorny ethical quandaries and alert us to institutional corruption. Unfortunately, it does a poor job. This time Edward Norton is the alienated cop, Ray Tierney. Like Max Payne, he's stepped away from the street to nurse his own grievances -- he bears an ugly scar down his cheek from an incident referred to only obliquely. The details remain hazy, but it casts a "Chinatown"-size cloud over Ray and probably accounts for the state of his marriage -- which is over -- and the fact that he's sleeping on his dad's leaky sailboat. There's considerably more plot in "Pride and Glory" than in "Max Payne," but it's only marginally less predictable. A shooting puts four cops down -- all of them from the command of Ray's brother Francis (Noah Emmerich). Francis is devastated, and the boys' father, Francis Sr. (Jon Voight), insists Ray must step up and take charge of the investigation. The Tierney clan has another cop in the family: Jimmy (Colin Farrell) is married to their sister (Lake Bell). We soon realize Jimmy's hands are dirty. But what will Ray do about it? If you've seen your Sidney Lumet movies -- "Serpico," "Prince of the City," "Q&A" -- then you'll be well ahead of the game. Even if you haven't, you'll have seen the cop shows that drew from them. Which is why almost every scene, every line of dialogue in "Pride and Glory" has the dull thud of cliche. "We can't keep doing this," moans Ray's soon-to-be ex-wife. Any regular moviegoer will know exactly what she means: How many more times will we have to suffer this déja-vu? Granted, originality isn't everything. Last year, James Grey's "We Own the Night" invested a very similar story with subtle character shadings and a subversive edge. What's most disappointing about O'Connor's capably acted but gloomy and portentous movie is how it shies away from any real complexity. The Tierneys may have their faults, but the outsider, Jimmy, is the bad egg (we gather that much when he threatens a baby with a hot iron). When push comes to shove, the brothers do the right thing in a climax so stock you could use it to make gravy. The old school was better than this. And, back then, it wasn't old either. "Pride and Glory," by contrast, stubbornly clings to tradition. Beyond not being drawn from a video game, you'd struggle to picture any of its characters ever touching one — or, for that matter, watching a film. Watch behind-the-scenes footage of "Pride and Glory."

Although the era is never spelled out, it feels like the present day trying to be 1974. Penned by Gavin O'Connor (who directed "Tumbleweeds") along with Joe Carnahan ("Narc"), and built on a premise O'Connor developed with his twin, Greg, and former NYPD officer Robert Hopes, this is the kind of picture aspiring to capture the earnest spirit of 1970s filmmaking — probing complicated moral dilemmas and exposing corruption within institutions. Sadly, it falls short.

Here, Edward Norton plays the disaffected officer, Ray Tierney. Much like Max Payne, he's pulled back from active duty to tend to his own wounds — a nasty scar runs down his cheek from an event that's only hinted at. "Pride and Glory" packs in far more story than "Max Payne," though it's only slightly less foreseeable. # The Uncertain Future of the Cop Thriller

Movie cop thrillers may be entering a period of decline, following a trajectory familiar to students of cinema history. Just as once-dominant genres like the musical and the western enjoyed decades of popularity before fading into relative obscurity during the 1970s, the police thriller now shows signs of the same waning cultural relevance. Genres, it seems, have life cycles, and the cop drama may be approaching the twilight of its own.

Two recent films illustrate the challenges facing the genre, each attempting a different strategy for survival—and each falling short in its own way.

## "Max Payne": Style Over Substance

"Max Payne," starring Mark Wahlberg as a police officer hunting down his family's killer, managed to top the box office despite a thoroughly predictable plot adapted from a video game. Rather than relying on the strength of its storytelling, the film leans almost entirely on visual style to captivate audiences.

The movie's appeal is fundamentally decorative. Its blue-filtered lighting and comic book-inspired compositions create a striking aesthetic surface, but these elements serve as substitutes for, rather than complements to, a compelling narrative. The result is a film that dazzles the eye while leaving the story disappointingly hollow—a triumph of atmosphere over meaning.

## "Pride and Glory": Ambition Without Execution

In stark contrast, "Pride and Glory" adopts an old-school sensibility, deliberately turning away from the video game influences that shaped films like "Max Payne." Instead, it aspires to emulate the serious, ethically complex cinema of the 1970s—that golden era of morally ambiguous crime dramas that grappled with weighty themes.

The film sets its sights on exploring institutional corruption and the difficult moral dilemmas faced by those who serve within compromised systems. Edward Norton appears as an alienated cop haunted by a mysterious past, a character type well-suited to such thematic ambitions.

Yet despite these lofty aspirations, "Pride and Glory" ultimately fails to execute its ideas effectively. The film gestures toward profundity but cannot deliver on its promises, leaving its serious themes underdeveloped and its dramatic potential unrealized.

## Conclusion

Together, these two films suggest a genre caught between competing impulses—one seduced by superficial style, the other reaching for a gravitas it cannot sustain. Whether the cop thriller can find a path forward, or whether it will follow the musical and the western into decline, remains an open question.

# Is the Police Thriller Dying?

The police thriller once occupied a central place in American cinema, but two recent films raise the uncomfortable question of whether the genre has run its course. Considered side by side, "Max Payne" and "Pride and Glory" represent two divergent responses to the challenge of keeping the police drama alive—and neither, ultimately, offers much reassurance about its future.

"Max Payne," adapted from the popular video game of the same name, embodies one possible direction: the surrender of storytelling to spectacle. The film is drenched in atmosphere, all rain-slicked streets, gothic shadows, and stylized violence rendered with the visual grammar of its interactive source material. Yet for all its surface sophistication, the film prioritizes look over logic. Plot becomes an afterthought, a thin scaffolding on which to hang one striking image after another. What emerges is a movie that dazzles the eye while leaving the mind unengaged—a police thriller in appearance only, hollowed out of the human stakes and narrative tension that once defined the form.

"Pride and Glory" takes the opposite approach, and in doing so reveals the genre's difficulties from the other end. Rather than reaching for novelty, the film reaches backward, deliberately styling itself after the grim, morally serious crime dramas that flourished in 1970s American cinema. This was an era when films about cops were willing to sit with discomfort—to examine institutional rot, the corrosive bonds of loyalty, and the ethical compromises demanded of those who wear the badge. "Pride and Glory" clearly aspires to join that tradition.

At the film's center stands Edward Norton's character, a detective set apart from those around him, alienated by his growing awareness of corruption within his own ranks—corruption that reaches into his own family. Through him, the film hopes to dramatize the collision between personal conscience and institutional complicity, to ask what a decent man owes to a system, and to the people, that have betrayed their principles. These are the very dilemmas that gave the classic police dramas their weight and lasting power.

But aspiration is not achievement. For all its evident sincerity and its earnest reaching toward gravity, "Pride and Glory" never fully delivers on its ambitions. The moral complexity it gestures toward remains more stated than felt, and the film finally falls short of the very tradition it seeks to honor.

Taken together, these two films suggest a genre caught between exhausted options—able neither to reinvent itself convincingly nor to recapture its former seriousness. It is a predicament that recalls the fate of other once-dominant forms. The musical and the western each reigned over the American screen before slipping, decade by decade, into irrelevance. Watching "Max Payne" and "Pride and Glory," one begins to wonder whether the police thriller is now approaching the same twilight.

# Blood Ties and Blue Lines: "Pride and Glory" Struggles to Rise Above Genre Conventions

**A Review**

Gavin O'Connor's "Pride and Glory" arrives carrying the weight of an impressive cast and a familiar burden: it's yet another gritty tale of police corruption, family loyalty, and the moral rot festering beneath the badge. The question isn't whether the film is competently made—it is—but whether it has anything new to say in a genre that has been mined so thoroughly it threatens to collapse under its own accumulated clichés.

## The Setup

The film centers on the Tierney family, a multi-generational NYPD dynasty. Jon Voight plays the patriarch, a police chief whose weathered face carries decades of institutional compromise. Noah Emmerich and Colin Farrell portray sons-in-law and brothers bound by blood and blue, while Edward Norton's Ray Tierney—the reluctant investigator—becomes the moral fulcrum when a botched drug raid leaves four officers dead and exposes a web of corruption reaching into his own family.

## Performances Carry the Weight

If "Pride and Glory" succeeds anywhere, it's in its performances. Norton brings his characteristic interiority to Ray, a man visibly corroding under the pressure of choosing between family and justice. Farrell is the film's dark engine—his Jimmy Egan radiates a dangerous charisma that curdles into genuine menace, particularly in an infamous scene involving a baby and a hot iron that pushes the film into truly disturbing territory. Voight, meanwhile, does reliable work as the compromised patriarch, though the role asks little the actor hasn't delivered before.

## The Genre Problem

Here's where the film stumbles. Watching "Pride and Glory," it's impossible not to feel the ghosts of superior predecessors. Sidney Lumet's "Serpico" and "Prince of the City" explored police corruption with far greater nuance decades earlier. James Gray's "We Own the Night" (released just a year prior) covered strikingly similar ground—cop families, divided loyalties, the crime-fighting bloodline. And Scorsese's "The Departed" had already demonstrated how to inject genuine tension and moral complexity into the corrupt-cop framework.

Against this lineage, O'Connor's film feels less like a fresh statement than a well-executed remix. The beats are predictable: the honest cop who discovers the rot, the fraternal confrontation, the climactic reckoning that pits blood against duty. We've walked these rain-slicked, morally ambiguous streets before.

## Is the Cop Thriller Becoming Outdated?

This brings us to a larger question the film inadvertently raises: has the gritty police drama exhausted itself?

The answer is more nuanced than a simple yes or no. The genre isn't dying so much as it's demanding reinvention. Films that merely rehearse the familiar iconography—the Irish-Catholic cop family, the thin blue line, the confessional-booth soul-searching—now feel like exercises in nostalgia rather than urgent drama. "Pride and Glory" belongs, unfortunately, to this category.

Yet the genre has proven remarkably adaptable when filmmakers are willing to interrogate rather than celebrate their subjects. The best recent entries succeed by complicating our relationship to police authority, reflecting evolving public attitudes toward institutional power. When a cop thriller engages honestly with systemic questions—rather than reducing corruption to a few bad apples in an otherwise noble family—it retains its power.

O'Connor's film gestures toward these deeper currents but ultimately retreats into melodrama, resolving its complexities through personal confrontation rather than sustained institutional critique. Its emotional climax—a literal bar fistfight between brothers—feels almost quaint, substituting physical catharsis for genuine reckoning.

## Verdict

"Pride and Glory" is a handsomely mounted, ably acted film that arrives too late to feel essential. Its strong performances and O'Connor's competent direction can't disguise a fundamental familiarity. Fans of the genre will find enough craftsmanship to justify a viewing, but those hoping for something that pushes the police drama forward will leave wanting.

The cop thriller isn't dead—but films like this suggest it needs to evolve or risk becoming a museum piece, endlessly polishing the same tarnished badge.

**★★½ out of five**

# Blood Thicker Than Justice: "Pride and Glory" Digs Into Familiar Territory

*A CNN Film Review*

There's a moment midway through Gavin O'Connor's "Pride and Glory" when Edward Norton, playing a detective forced to investigate corruption within his own police family, stares into the middle distance with the weary look of a man who knows the truth will cost him everything. It's a beautiful, aching beat—the kind of morally exhausted performance that recalls the golden age of American crime drama. If only the film surrounding it lived up to that promise.

## An Old Story, Well-Worn

"Pride and Glory" follows the Tierney clan, a multi-generational family of New York cops whose loyalty is tested when a drug raid leaves four officers dead. Norton's Ray Tierney is pulled from a comfortable desk assignment to lead the investigation, while his brother-in-law Jimmy (a menacing Colin Farrell) sits at the rotten center of the department's dark secrets.

The DNA here is unmistakably Lumet. "Serpico" and "Prince of the City" hang over this film like ghosts, and O'Connor clearly aspires to that tradition of institutional rot and personal reckoning. The blue-collar Catholic milieu, the sense of the badge as both blessing and curse—these are the textures of 1970s crime cinema at its finest.

## Where It Stumbles

Unfortunately, aspiration and achievement are different animals.

Where Lumet trusted his audiences with moral ambiguity, "Pride and Glory" too often reaches for melodrama. A subplot involving a threatened infant crosses from tension into exploitation. The film's grimy handheld aesthetic sometimes feels less like authenticity and more like affectation.

Which brings us to "Max Payne," the other cop-adjacent thriller haunting the multiplex this season. That film—also starring a brooding lead navigating conspiracy—traded entirely on style over substance, drowning its noir ambitions in video-game visual excess. "Pride and Glory" is unquestionably the more serious and better-acted picture. But both share a common failure: they mistake grim atmosphere for genuine gravity.

## The Saving Grace

What elevates "Pride and Glory" above genre disposability is its cast. Norton grounds every scene in lived-in weariness. Farrell finds unexpected pathos in a man who has convinced himself his crimes are protective acts of love. Jon Voight, as the family patriarch, brings a boozy grandeur that feels transported directly from a different, perhaps better film.

## The Verdict

"Pride and Glory" is a frustrating experience—a movie with the ambitions of "Prince of the City" and the execution of a well-above-average television procedural. It reaches for the moral complexity of Lumet and grasps something considerably more conventional.

Still, for viewers hungry for adult drama in a season of comic-book spectacle and "Max Payne"-style pyrotechnics, there's genuine craft here worth appreciating—even when the film can't quite escape the long shadows of its betters.

**Rating: 2.5 out of 4 stars**

---

*"Pride and Glory" is rated R for strong violence, pervasive language, and brief drug content. Running time: 130 minutes.*

# Pride and Glory: A Familiar Beat

There's a specific texture to the great '70s cop films—the sweaty moral ambiguity of *Serpico*, the institutional rot of *The French Connection*, the sense that the city itself is a character that grinds people down. "Pride and Glory" clearly wants to inherit that lineage, and to its credit, it understands the assignment even when it can't quite complete it.

## The Plot

The film centers on the Tierney family, a multigenerational NYPD dynasty. When four officers are killed in a Washington Heights drug bust gone catastrophically wrong, detective Ray Tierney is pulled into the investigation. What he uncovers is a corruption scheme reaching into his own family—specifically implicating his brother-in-law Jimmy, who runs a crew of cops operating well outside the law. The story becomes a slow-motion collision between blood loyalty and the badge, staged against a wintry, unglamorous New York.

## The Cast

This is where the film earns its keep. **Edward Norton** plays Ray with a coiled, interior restraint—a man doing math he doesn't want to finish. **Colin Farrell** is genuinely unsettling as Jimmy, charismatic and monstrous in roughly equal measure (an interrogation-adjacent scene involving an infant and a hot iron is the film's most notorious). **Jon Voight** anchors the older generation as the family patriarch, all whiskey and weathered compromise, and **Noah Emmerich** rounds out the brothers with quiet decency.

## Fresh or Cliched?

Honestly, a bit of both—leaning cliched.

**What works** is the mood and the moral weight. The film takes seriously the idea that corruption is rarely cartoonish; it's a series of small accommodations that harden into something unforgivable. That's very much in the '70s spirit, which resisted clean heroes.

**What doesn't** is that the beats are deeply familiar. The honest-cop-versus-dirty-family framework has been worn smooth by everything from *Prince of the City* to the *Departed*-era wave of the 2000s. You can often see the plot's next move coming, and the film occasionally reaches for operatic confrontation (including a climactic bar brawl) where the older classics would have trusted silence and ambiguity.

## The Verdict

"Pride and Glory" is a well-acted, grim, respectable entry that honors the tradition without meaningfully extending it. Where *Serpico* felt dangerous and *The French Connection* felt documentary-raw, this feels *composed*—a genre exercise executed by people who love the genre. That's not nothing. But it's homage rather than evolution.

**Three out of five badges.** Worth watching for the performances and the atmosphere; just don't expect it to reinvent the beat it walks.

# Blood and Badge: A Review of *Pride and Glory*

Some films arrive with the weight of expectation and the burden of familiarity. *Pride and Glory*, Gavin O'Connor's grim procedural about police corruption within a family of New York City cops, is one such film—a picture so committed to its bleak vision of institutional rot that it occasionally forgets to surprise us along the way. What it lacks in narrative innovation, however, it partially recovers through committed performances and a genuine willingness to sit in moral discomfort.

## A Family Divided

The premise is engineered for maximum ethical tension. The Tierney clan is a multigenerational police family: patriarch Francis Sr. (Jon Voight) presides over a legacy that his sons and son-in-law are meant to uphold. When a botched drug bust leaves four officers dead, Ray Tierney (Edward Norton) is pulled into the investigation, only to discover that the corruption trail leads uncomfortably close to home—specifically to his brother-in-law Jimmy Egan (Colin Farrell).

This is where the film earns its keep. *Pride and Glory* is fundamentally interested in the collision between two competing loyalties: the code of family and the code of law. It asks whether blood should ever trump justice, and whether the "thin blue line" becomes a form of tribalism when officers protect their own at the expense of the citizens they serve. The film refuses easy answers, and to its credit, it doesn't fully absolve anyone. Even the ostensibly noble Ray is compromised by his hesitation, his complicity in silence, and his understanding of how the machine works.

## The Weight of Predictability

Here is the film's central weakness: you can see nearly every beat coming. From the moment the corruption is introduced, the trajectory is telegraphed. We know the good brother will be forced to confront the bad one. We know the patriarch will be caught between paternal love and institutional duty. We know there will be a reckoning, and we can guess roughly what shape it will take.

The screenplay leans heavily on genre conventions that anyone who has watched a police drama will recognize instantly. The corrupt-cop-crisis narrative has been explored more sharply elsewhere, and *Pride and Glory* doesn't bring enough fresh perspective to distinguish itself from its predecessors. Its predictability isn't fatal, but it does drain tension from sequences that should feel more urgent. When the destination is never in doubt, the journey has to work harder—and here it only partly succeeds.

## Performances That Elevate the Material

If the plot feels well-worn, the acting frequently transcends it. Edward Norton brings his characteristic interiority to Ray, playing a man wrestling with his conscience through quiet, watchful restraint rather than histrionics. It's a performance built on hesitation and moral fatigue, and Norton makes Ray's internal conflict feel lived-in.

Colin Farrell, meanwhile, is the film's most volatile asset. His Jimmy Egan is charming and monstrous in roughly equal measure, and one particularly disturbing scene involving a threat to an infant remains genuinely hard to watch. Farrell resists the temptation to play a cartoon villain; instead, he shows us a man who has rationalized his corruption as a form of provision and loyalty, which is far more unsettling.

Jon Voight, chewing scenery as the whiskey-soaked patriarch, is somewhat broader, but he lends the film a mythic, almost tragic weight. The family dynamics feel authentic largely because the cast commits so fully to the pained, coded ways these men communicate.

## Final Verdict

*Pride and Glory* is a flawed but frequently gripping drama that succeeds more on the strength of its performances and its willingness to grapple with genuine ethical weight than on any narrative originality. It won't surprise you, but it may still disturb you—and in a genre this crowded, that counts for something. Viewers seeking a morally complex character study will find enough here to justify the watch, even if those hoping for narrative innovation walk away disappointed.

**Rating: 3 out of 5 stars**

**Runtime: 130 minutes**

# The Fading Badge: Is the Cop Thriller Following Westerns into the Sunset?

There was a time when the cop thriller stood as one of Hollywood's most reliable engines—a genre that gave us the sweaty paranoia of *Serpico*, the moral rot of *Prince of the City*, and the operatic corruption of *L.A. Confidential*. Yet watching recent entries like *Max Payne* (2008) and *Pride and Glory* (2008), one gets the uneasy sense that this genre may be approaching the same twilight that claimed the Western and the movie musical—not dead, but increasingly a relic, wheeled out of storage more from habit than genuine cultural need.

## The Symptoms of Decline

Genres don't die because filmmakers stop making them. They die when they run out of new things to say, when the formula calcifies into self-parody, and when audiences can predict every beat before the credits roll. The Western didn't vanish because horses went out of style; it faded because its mythology of frontier justice stopped resonating with a nation that had grown skeptical of its own origin stories. The musical collapsed when audiences no longer accepted characters bursting into song as an emotional shorthand.

Both *Pride and Glory* and *Max Payne* display the warning signs of a genre exhausting itself.

## *Pride and Glory*: The Weight of Familiarity

*Pride and Glory*, directed by Gavin O'Connor, is in many ways a competently made film. It boasts a strong cast—Edward Norton, Colin Farrell, Jon Voight—and it takes seriously the genre's core preoccupations: the corruption within the ranks, the tension between family loyalty and institutional duty, the blue wall of silence. The problem is that we have seen all of this before, and done better.

The film feels less like a fresh statement than an anthology of gestures borrowed from superior predecessors. The corrupt cop tempted by dirty money, the honest detective who must expose his own kin, the confrontation between duty and blood—these were fresh in *Serpico* and *The Departed*, but here they arrive pre-worn. O'Connor directs with sincerity, yet sincerity cannot compensate for the sense of déjà vu. When Farrell's character crosses his moral lines, we register the beats not as revelations but as inevitabilities. This is the sound of a genre spinning its wheels: technically proficient, emotionally muted, saying nothing new about the world it depicts.

## *Max Payne*: Genre Dissolving into Spectacle

If *Pride and Glory* represents the exhaustion of the cop thriller through repetition, *Max Payne* represents something arguably worse—the genre's dissolution into other forms entirely. Adapted from a video game, the film wears the trappings of the tormented-cop narrative (the murdered family, the vengeance quest, the noir shadows), but it has little interest in the genre's actual concerns of institutional morality and procedural detail. Instead, it drifts into a stylized realm of Valkyrie hallucinations, supernatural imagery, and comic-book aesthetics.

This is telling. When a genre can no longer sustain itself on its own terms, it becomes a costume for other, more commercially vibrant forms—here, the video-game adaptation and the action spectacle. *Max Payne* uses the cop thriller as a skin stretched over an entirely different creature. The Western underwent a similar mutation in its decline, morphing into science-fiction (*Outland*) and revisionist deconstructions before largely retreating from mainstream production. When the essential DNA of a genre must be diluted to survive, its identity is already dissolving.

## The Counter-Argument

It would be premature, however, to sign the death certificate. The cop thriller possesses one advantage that Westerns and musicals lacked: its subject matter—crime, justice, corruption, the moral cost of law enforcement—remains perpetually relevant. The relationship between police and the public is, if anything, more culturally charged now than in decades past. This means the genre retains a wellspring of urgency that the frontier myth eventually lost.

Moreover, the genre has proven remarkably adaptable to television, where the long-form format allows the procedural depth and moral complexity that films increasingly abandon. Perhaps the cop thriller isn't dying so much as migrating.

## Conclusion: A Genre in Purgatory

*Max Payne* and *Pride and Glory* together suggest a genre caught in a transitional purgatory. One film shows us exhaustion through slavish imitation; the other shows us dilution through hybridization. Neither offers the vital, urgent statement that once defined the form at its best. In this sense, the cop thriller does exhibit the classic symptoms that preceded the retreat of the Western and the musical.

Yet the genre's raw material remains too socially potent to disappear entirely. The badge may be fading, but it has not yet been retired. What these films truly reveal is not death but drift—a genre that has lost its sense of purpose and is waiting, perhaps, for a filmmaker bold enough to remind us why it mattered in the first place.
